forbidden_subjects: a landlord character, or any framing of a greedy private landlord — the defendant was the Housing Authority of Louisville, a government body
an eviction in progress: furniture on a pavement, a family being put out, a sheriff at a door
any depiction of the three named appellees or their homes
any likeness of the real people named in the record
readable text, numerals, signage, logos, seals or emblems in any generated image
courtroom interiors, gavels, judges' benches — 23 of 24 archive courtroom clips are already used in earlier episodes and the look is spent
prison cells, bars, razor wire, handcuffs — 18-24 of 24 already used, and none of these episodes is about incarceration
any real building, hospital, courthouse or housing project identifiable by signage or architecture
stock-photo emotion: a hand on a shoulder, a tear, a clock ticking down, a gavel falling
forbidden_claims: Any sentence of the form "today a landlord can still just tape a paper to your door". The case is from 1982 and this ledger establishes nothing about current practice.
"Because of this case, every State now has to mail eviction notices." Not what the Court held.
"The Supreme Court banned posting." It did not.
Any national number — how many evictions, how many default judgments, how many tenants never see the notice. The opinion gives none.
"They lost their homes" / any account of what happened to Linnie Lindsey, Barbara Hodgens or Pamela Ray afterwards. The opinion does not say.
"She never saw the notice" stated as established fact. It is an allegation at summary judgment, never a finding.
Any claim about the landlord's motive — greed, retaliation, serving when nobody was home on purpose.
Confusing Lindsey v. Normet, 405 U.S. 56 (1972) with the appellee Linnie Lindsey.
"The tenants won their case" / "the Supreme Court gave them their homes back."

CASE: Greene v. Lindsey, 456 U.S. 444 (1982)
FACTS: episodes/_planning/EP62_greene_FACTS_LEDGER.v001.md

REGISTER: the defendant is a public housing authority, so this is a story about a government's own notice procedure, not about a landlord. Every draft that reaches for the greedy-landlord frame is factually wrong and must be rewritten.

The strongest verbatim in the ledger is GL-56: posting on an apartment door does not satisfy minimum standards of due process because in a significant number of instances it fails to give actual notice. The dissent (O'CONNOR, joined by the Chief Justice and Rehnquist -- an earlier note in this file said Stevens, which was wrong; Stevens does not appear in this opinion at all and his dissent belongs to EP64 Memphis Light. Corrected 2026-08-04 against the opinion text) is quotable and should be used — it argues the Court preferred the Postal Service on no evidence about the mails. A one-sided film here is a weaker film.
